<Rep. Jamie Raskin>: As co-Chair of the Animal Protection Caucus and a huge dog person, I've taken a strong interest in this bill and the case underlying it.
The case illustrates the cavalier violent abuse of animals we see everywhere. Alas, the bill is also a great example of a trend both parties have opposed: duplicating existing offenses and filling the books with redundant statutes.
This bill all started when canine detective Freddie the Beagle, who was working with the U.S. Customs and Border Protection to detect smuggled agricultural products at Washington Dulles International Airport, repeatedly barked and alerted his commanding officers to the presence of over 100 pounds of prohibited food items in bags unloading at the luggage pickup area. The prohibited food items belonged to Hamed Ramadan Bayoumy Aly Marie, age 70, a traveler and foreign national from Egypt.\1\
\1\U.S. Customs and Border Protection, Local Media Release: Egyptian Traveler Eats Federal Charges for Kicking Dulles CBP Beagle that Detected over 100 Pounds of Prohibited Food Products (June 26, 2025), https://www.cbp.gov/newsroom/local-media-release/egyptian-traveler-eats-federal-charges-kicking-dulles-cbp-beagle.
Apparently frustrated and angry over the dog's excellent detective work, Mr. Marie kicked Freddie so hard he became airborne and suffered bruised ribs. If you're an animal lover like me, surely you say, ``That should be illegal!'' And sure enough, it was.
Mr. Marie was arrested and held by the police for several days and then pleaded guilty to one count of harming animals used in law enforcement under 18 U.S.C. Sec. 1368.\2\ He was convicted and sentenced to time served and ordered to pay for the animal's veterinarian bill, which court records show was $840.\3\ Apparently, Freddie the Dog is doing fine, and Mr. Marie was deported back to Egypt after the court hearing.\4\
\2\Id.
\3\Hannah Sampson, Man Who Kicked Customs Dog at Dulles Ordered to Leave U.S., Wash. Post (June 27, 2025), https://www.washingtonpost.com/ travel/2025/06/27/freddie-dog-kicked-cbp-dulles/.
\4\Id.
Thus, as just vividly demonstrated, this conduct is already criminally proscribed and the basis for removal of a noncitizen. It is against the law now to kick the police dog, and Mr. Marie won himself three days in jail for doing it.
But the opportunity to introduce a redundant bill is apparently impossible for politicians to pass up, which is an occupational hazard. H.R. 4638 would render inadmissible and deportable any noncitizen who willfully or maliciously harms a police dog or a police horse.
I am unaware of any mad rush of immigrants roaming the country and attacking police animals, so I am not sure what crisis this surplus language is responding to. In any event, what should have happened here did happen here. Mr. Marie was criminally charged, prosecuted, convicted, and deported from the country. In other words, the criminal justice system and the immigration system worked just like they are supposed to--a foreign national committed a crime, he was arrested, charged, prosecuted, convicted, and removed from the country, all without being stripped of any of the due process protections afforded to people in our country.
All I see this bill doing is short-circuiting the need to actually prosecute someone for an alleged assault. This bill would render not just a vacation traveler but a green card holder deportable for kicking a police animal even if she or he is never arrested, prosecuted or convicted of that crime.
I want to be clear about how absurd this is. There is no crime so serious that people don't actually have to be prosecuted for it before punishment. If a citizen or a green card holder murders someone, we require that they be convicted prior to being sent to prison or rendered deportable.
If this bill were to become law, individuals accused of attacking police animals will be treated in the immigration system more harshly than people accused of murdering a human being. That just makes no sense and will stick out like a sore thumb.
Under the Immigration and Nationality Act, a noncitizen convicted of a Crime Involving Moral Turpitude, or a ``CIMT,'' is automatically deportable. There are a wide variety of CIMTs, including affirmative acts to impede law enforcement and acts that harm animals. In 2018, the Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA) found that the crime of animal fighting is a CIMT because there is a clear intent to harm the animal.\5\ The BIA noted that to ``constitute a crime involving moral turpitude, an offense must have two essential elements: a culpable mental state and reprehensible conduct.''\6\
\5\Matter of Ortega-Lopez, 27 I&N Dec. 382 (BIA 2018).
\6\Id.
The Administrative Appeals Office (AAO) for United States Citizenship and Immigration Services also reached a similar conclusion when assessing whether an individual could meet the requirement for good moral character given that they were convicted under a state statute related to animal cruelty.\7\ The AAO found that the ``statute under which the petitioner was convicted prescribes a mens rea of intentional commission of an act to an animal, which causes or results in the cruel death, or excessive or repeated infliction of unnecessary pain or suffering'' and that this ``criminal intent meets the test for moral turpitude. . . .''\8\ As such, the AAO found that the individual was not a person of good moral character due to his conviction of a CIMT.\9\ The mens rea requirement in 18 U.S.C.
Sec. 1368 is very similar to both these cases and thus would likely qualify the conduct as a CIMT.
\7\See Administrative Appeals Office decision EAC0425553110, at https://www.uscis.gov/sites/ default/files/err/ B9%20%20Battered%20Spouse%20or%20Child/Decisions-Issued-in-2006/May23 2006-03B9204.pdf.
\8\Id.
\9\Id.
As such, conviction for harming a police animal, the conduct this bill attempts to discourage, is already a deportable offense. The key point here is that currently, only individuals who are convicted of such a crime are rendered deportable. This bill eliminates the conviction requirement, and in so doing, violates bedrock principles of fairness and due process, and ensuring that people have their day in court. This bill erodes the due process rights enshrined in the Constitution that are so fundamental to our legal system.
This legislation puts us on a slippery slope of chipping away at due process rights for all. I oppose this legislation, and I urge my colleagues to do the same.
Jamie Raskin,
Ranking Member.
